Authors: Hoveling LA, Bergink-Voorthuis BJ, van Vlaardingen JRG, Verhoeven RHA, Wagner AD, Soerjomataram I, Siesling S
Journal: ESMO real world data and digital oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100790
Published: 2026-Dec-01
PMID: 42959695



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We analysed sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality using a national development index to better understand how broader socioeconomic factors may contribute to or mitigate sex differences in cancer outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Cancer incidence and mortality data (2012-2017) were obtained from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, covering 43 countries for incidence and 60 for mortality. Only nonsex-specific cancers were included and categorised into 12 groups. Age-standardised incidence rates (ASIR) and age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) were calculated, with sex differences analysed using men-to-women ratios (MWRs). Linear regression was used to assess the association between Human Development Index (HDI) and MWRs across cancer types. RESULTS: Among the cancer types included in this study, cancers of the colorectum, stomach, and lungs showed the highest incidence and mortality. Men are 12-13 times more likely to be diagnosed with oesophageal cancer (MWR ≈ 13), over nine times more likely to die from head and neck cancers, and >6 times more likely to die from lung cancer. Thyroid cancer incidence is up to five times higher in women than in men. No clear link was found between HDI and MWRs in incidence, but HDI relates to mortality and MWRs for several cancer types, with brain and thyroid cancers showing higher male mortality, while lung cancer showing relatively higher female mortality in high-HDI countries. CONCLUSIONS: Sex differences in cancer burden vary substantially across cancer types. National development was associated with sex differences in mortality, but not incidence, suggesting that factors related to health care and survival differ more between countries with different HDIs and contribute to these differences more than exposure to risk factors, which relates more to incidence.

Authors: Han Y, Yi X, Xia J, Zhang W, Zhao Z, Zhu N, Liu N, Chen X, Wang Y, Feng L, et al.
Journal: BMJ (Clinical research ed.) | DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2026-101019
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42982504



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess the effect of ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) compared with endotracheal tube (ETT) on perioperative respiratory adverse events (PRAEs) in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. DESIGN: Multicentre, randomised, parallel group trial. SETTING: Four tertiary hospitals in China, 2023-24. PARTICIPANTS: 400 children aged ≥2 years and <7 years who were scheduled for adenotonsillectomy under general anaesthesia. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomised 1:1 to receive ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (n=200) or an endotracheal tube (n=200) during adenotonsillectomy. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The primary outcome was the proportion of participants who developed any perioperative respiratory adverse event (PRAE): laryngospasm, bronchospasm, desaturation, airway obstruction, severe cough, or stridor in the intention-to-treat population. RESULTS: 400 children (mean age 4.7 (standard deviation 1.0) years; 155 (38.7%) girls) were enrolled between 24 May 2023 and 4 April 2024, with last follow-up on 4 May 2024. LMA was converted to ETT in three participants. Overall, 22.5% (45/200) participants in the LMA group experienced PRAEs versus 57.5% (115/200) in the ETT group (absolute risk difference -35.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval -43.5 to -25.7; P<0.001). The LMA group had fewer PRAEs in both the intraoperative (9.0% (18/200) v 17.5% (35/200); -8.5, -15.2 to -1.8; P=0.01) and the postoperative period (16.5% (33/200) v 49.5% (99/200); -33.0, -41.2 to -24.0; P<0.001). The LMA group also had a lower proportion of participants with laryngospasm (0.0% v 3.0%; P=0.03), desaturation (15.0% v 28.0%; P=0.002), airway obstruction (3.5% v 12.5%; P<0.001), and severe cough (10.5% v 42.0%; P<0.001). Neither group experienced serious adverse events. CONCLUSION: Ventilation with an LMA by experienced anaesthesiologists resulted in fewer perioperative respiratory adverse events than ventilation with an ETT in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chictr.org.cn ChiCTR2300071399.

Authors: Shi X, Liu Q, Xu B, Li D, Matrone A, Hadoux J, Ganly I, Houot B, Zheng X, Wohllk N, et al.
Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology | DOI: 10.1200/JCO-26-01146
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42981561



Abstract:
PURPOSE: To refine the suboptimal prognostic discrimination of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM (TNM-8) staging system for medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients with MTC from 43 centers across 15 countries under the framework of the International Medullary Thyroid Cancer Staging Consortium (IMTCSC). Pooled data were analyzed with disease-specific survival as the primary end point. With M1 disease fixed in stage IVC, we redefined the schema for stages I to IVB in M0 patients. Using exhaustive enumeration, all possible TN combinations were fitted into multivariable Cox models, with the lowest Akaike information criterion (AIC) defining the proposed system. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and the concordance index (C-index). RESULTS: The IMTCSC cohort included 2,573 patients with MTC (female-to-male ratio: 1.25; median age 52 years [IQR, 41-62]; median follow-up 76.3 months [IQR, 37.3-121.0]). Level VII metastasis correlated with poorer survival, supporting its upgrade to N1c. Exhaustive search of 116,284 admissible stage-grouping schemas identified the optimal model (lowest AIC) defining stages I to IVB: I (T1N0-N1a/T2N0), II (T1N1b/T2N1a/T3N0), III (T1N1c/T2N1b/T3N1a/T4aN0-N1a), IVA (T2N1c/T3N1b-N1c/T4aN1b), and IVB (T4aN1c/T4b any N). Compared with AJCC TNM-8 (stage I as reference; stage II aHR, 0.84, P = .652; stage III aHR, 1.48, P = .172; stage IV aHR, 7.95, P < .001), the proposed system showed a clearer monotonic increase in disease-specific death risk (stage II aHR 2.22; stage III aHR, 4.81; stage IV aHR 15.75; all P ≤ .001) and a higher C-index (0.892 v 0.856, P < .001), which was also evaluated in the SEER cohort (N = 1,909). CONCLUSION: The proposed MTC staging system confers an improved schema for prognostic stratification compared with AJCC TNM-8.

Authors: Akdogan O, Yesilbas E, Yılmaz M, Keskin Uzundere F, Oruc A, Ozcelik EE, Turhan G, Kayaalp M, Deliktas Onur I, Temizyurek H, et al.
Journal: JCO oncology practice | DOI: 10.1200/OP-26-00226
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42981536



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Regorafenib-induced hand-foot skin reaction (HFSR) is a common dose-limiting toxicity. We evaluated whether prophylaxis with oral zinc plus topical clobetasol is associated with lower clinically significant HFSR compared with either strategy alone. METHODS: ZINCLO-HAND was a prospective, multicenter, pragmatic, nonrandomized comparative study across 13 oncology centers in Türkiye. Adults initiating regorafenib were managed at physician discretion with oral zinc, topical clobetasol propionate 0.05%, or the combination for 8 weeks. The primary end point was grade ≥2 HFSR within the prophylaxis period. Secondary end points included grade 3 HFSR, treatment modification, relative dose intensity, and patient-reported outcomes. RESULTS: Of 179 enrolled patients, 156 were evaluable: zinc, n = 49; clobetasol, n = 52; combination, n = 55. Grade ≥2 HFSR occurred in 38.8%, 38.5%, and 16.4% of patients, respectively (P = .016). In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, tumor type, and initial regorafenib dose intensity, zinc monotherapy (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 3.37 [95% CI, 1.30 to 8.71]; P = .012) and clobetasol monotherapy (adjusted OR, 3.15 [95% CI, 1.26 to 7.88]; P = .014) were associated with higher odds of grade ≥2 HFSR versus combination prophylaxis. Median relative dose intensity was comparable across groups. HFSR-attributable treatment modification occurred in 30.6%, 28.8%, and 12.7% of patients, respectively. CONCLUSION: In this nonrandomized prospective cohort, zinc plus topical clobetasol was associated with lower clinically significant regorafenib-induced HFSR and fewer HFSR-attributable treatment modifications. These findings support consideration of combination prophylaxis in routine practice and warrant randomized confirmation.

Authors: Chen YC, Liao WL, Wang SC, Tai CH
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359955
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42981285



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To minimize environmental services staff's exposure to pathogens, ultraviolet-C (UV-C) disinfection robots were applied before terminal manual environmental disinfection. This study aimed to evaluate the disinfection efficacy of the UV-C robot and to assess the effects of ultraviolet-C dose, distance, and direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) on disinfection outcomes. METHODS: This before-after study was conducted in a negative-pressure isolation ward comprising 17 single-patient rooms at a medical center in Taiwan between August 24, 2024, and January 3, 2025, yielding a total of 270 paired samples. An ultraviolet-C-emitting robot with a wavelength of 254 nm was sequentially positioned on both sides of the patient bed and operated for 5 minutes on each side before routine manual environmental disinfection. Total aerobic colony counts (ACC) and bacterial culture positivity rates were obtained from high-touch environmental surfaces (e.g., bed rails, call bells and bedside chairs) before and after UV-C disinfection. The effects of UV-C dose, distance between the robot and surfaces, and the presence of direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) versus indirect exposure on disinfection efficacy were analyzed using multivariate binary logistic regression, performed using SPSS version 27.0. The results of the regression analysis were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: The median ACC and bacterial culture positivity rates on surfaces significantly decreased after UV-C disinfection (0.76 vs. 0.08 CFU/cm²; 83% vs. 57.4%, P < 0.001). A weak negative correlation was observed between ACC and UV-C doses after disinfection (rs = -0.281, 95% CI: -0.390 to -0.164, P < 0.001), while no correlation (rs = 0.040, 95% CI: -0.083 to 0.162, P = 0.510) and weak correlation (rs = 0.317, 95% CI: 0.202 to 0.424, P <  0.001) were found between ACC at short and long irradiation distances. The ACC on environmental surfaces with direct UV-C exposure were significantly lower than those in shadowed areas [median: 0.00 (IQR: 0.00 to 0.44) vs. median: 0.16 (IQR: 0.00 to 0.80); P < 0.001]. Multivariate logistic regression identified direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) as the strongest predictor of negative bacterial culture results, reducing the odds of bacterial culture positivity by 79.5% compared to indirect exposure (OR = 0.205, 95% CI: 0.083 to 0.508, P < 0.001) in the layout of the negative pressure isolation room in this study. CONCLUSIONS: Ultraviolet-C robots serve as an effective disinfection intervention for hospital environments. Their efficacy is most pronounced when direct exposure (line-of-sight irradiation) is achieved in the isolation rooms. Therefore, aligning movable items toward the UV-C robot prior to disinfection, alongside subsequent manual environmental disinfection and physical debris removal, remains essential, particularly in shadowed areas.

Authors: Rajan A, Biji CL, Sinha MG, Oviya IR
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360612
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42981280



Abstract:
The precise classification of basal, classical, atypical, and mesenchymal subtypes of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (HNSCC) is crucial for advancing precision oncology. Our research aims to develop an explainable subtype classification model for HNSCC.These molecular subtypes have been previously defined; reliable and meaningful computational methods for the classification of molecular subtypes and prioritization of molecular biomarkers for each subtype do not exist. We developed an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model that classifies molecular subtypes based on combined transcriptomic profiles from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-HNSC) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE65858). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to quantify the importance of genes for model predictions. Subsequently, genes with high predictive importance were analyzed in protein-protein interactions using STRING, and hub genes were identified by Maximum Clique Centrality (MCC) and used for the identification of candidate biomarkers for each of the subtypes. We employed machine learning methods such as Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), AdaBoost (AB), Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), XGBoost (XGB), and Gradient Boosting (GB). The XGBoost model achieved an accuracy of 95% after hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation. Biologically relevant subtype-specific biomarkers associated with each molecular subtype were identified. To highlight the potential biological functions of these biomarkers, pathway analysis was performed. Further assessment of these genes, such as survival analysis and druggability, showed promise for the development of targeted therapies.

Authors: Fenech AL, Park ER, Wirth LJ, D'Souza G, Humphris G, Siegel SD, Pring M, Laurenceau JP
Journal: Journal of cancer survivorship : research and practice | DOI: 10.1007/s11764-026-02146-7
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42980934



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) experience substantial symptom burden related to both disease and intensive treatments. Understanding long-term symptom patterns may help identify patients at risk for persistent emotional and physical symptom burden. This study evaluated symptom trajectories of anxiety, depression, fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), and oral pain among patients with HNC from diagnosis through long-term survivorship. METHODS: This secondary analysis included 5411 patients with HNC from the Head and Neck 5000 study in the UK. Latent class growth analysis (LCGA) and growth mixture modeling (GMM) were used to examine changes in symptoms, predictors of class membership, and within-class variability. RESULTS: The majority of patients were classified into a mild symptom class for depression (58%), anxiety (48%), and oral pain (62%), whereas the largest FCR class (44%) represented moderate symptoms. Anxiety, FCR, and oral pain followed recovery trajectories characterized by symptom improvement, while depression demonstrated a distinct pattern of worsening symptoms. Across symptoms, nearly 20% of patients belonged to an elevated symptom trajectory. These patients were more likely to be younger in age, have lower income, and report greater weekly alcohol consumption. Patients with HPV-positive HNC experienced faster reductions in anxiety and FCR but greater increases in depression over time. CONCLUSIONS: Distinct symptom trajectories were observed into long-term survivorship among patients with HNC. Although most patients experienced mild-to-moderate symptoms, a clinically important subgroup remained at elevated risk for persistent symptoms. IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: Early identification of patients at risk for persistent symptoms may facilitate targeted supportive care and behavioral interventions to improve long-term survivorship outcomes.

Authors: Pandey A, Pandey L, Mishra V, Singh P, Kunduru HPR, Lohia S, Pasricha R, Pasricha Y
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70537
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42980345



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a readily measured indicator of nutritional status; however, its impact on outcomes in head and neck cancer (HNC) patients remains understudied. This study evaluated the impact of pre-treatment BMI on toxicities and survival in such patients. METHODS: This retrospective study included 212 patients of locally advanced HNC treated with definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy or radiotherapy alone. Patients were categorized into BMI < 25 kg/m2 and ≥ 25 kg/m2. Toxicities were assessed using CTCAE v5.0. Overall survival (OS) and locoregional control (LRC) were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method. RESULTS: Eighty-six percent of patients had BMI of < 25Kg/m2. These patients experienced significantly higher rates of grade ≥ 2 mucositis, dermatitis, candidiasis, and greater need for nutritional support (44.7%; p = 0.039). Median OS and LRC were 25 and 24 months, respectively. Three-year OS and LRC were 46.3% and 39%. BMI category, T stage, and nodal stage independently predicted OS. CONCLUSION: BMI < 25 Kg/m2 patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy or radiotherapy alone are more prone to treatment-related toxicities and have inferior survival outcomes. Early nutritional assessment and intervention should be integrated into routine management to improve treatment outcomes.

Authors: Najjar E, Abdelraziq M, Yaniv D, Ritter A, Abu-Elnaaj I, Ghantous Y
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70534
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42979766



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effect of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) by evaluating its impact on surgical efficiency and postoperative morbidity in patients undergoing complex free-flap reconstruction for advanced oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). METHODS: A retrospective comparative study was conducted on 86 patients (NACT cohort: n = 20; Primary Surgery cohort: n = 66) undergoing microvascular free tissue transfer. Primary outcomes included surgical efficiency (ischemic time, total operative duration) and postoperative complications (major microvascular events vs. minor wound issues) that were evaluated. RESULTS: The NACT group presented with significantly more advanced disease (100% Stage IV vs. 39.4%; p < 0.001). Despite this higher tumor burden, the NACT cohort demonstrated significantly shorter mean ischemic times (39.0 ± 7.5 vs. 52.5 ± 17.9 min; p = 0.001) and reduced operative durations (7.5 ± 0.8 vs. 8.6 ± 1.3 h; p = 0.001). Total complication rates were comparable (35% vs. 33.3%). However, minor wound-related complications were significantly more frequent in the NACT group (30% vs. 4.5%; p = 0.004). The flap salvage rate following re-exploration was high and comparable between groups (80.0% vs. 85.7%). CONCLUSION: No statistically significant differences were detected in major flap failure or vascular re-exploration, though the study was underpowered to establish definitive safety equivalence for these endpoints. In exploratory subgroup analysis of RFFF reconstructions, NACT was associated with reduced ischemic time (p = 0.017). These findings suggest that while NACT compromises soft-tissue wound healing, it does not preclude successful microvascular reconstruction when managed with appropriate perioperative care.

Authors: Singh A, Chaturvedi P
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70534
Published: 2026-Nov-04
PMID: 42979722



Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Locally advanced oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains surgically anchored, but systemic treatment is evolving rapidly, particularly with perioperative immunotherapy. METHODS: We reviewed clinical evidence on neoadjuvant, adjuvant, maintenance, and altered-dose systemic strategies for resectable locally advanced OSCC and relevant head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. RESULTS: Conventional neoadjuvant chemotherapy has not improved survival in unselected resectable OSCC and should be reserved for selected indications including borderline resectability, mandibular preservation, and conversion to surgery. Neoadjuvant immunotherapy studies using PD-1 blockade, dual checkpoint inhibition, chemoimmunotherapy, targeted-immunotherapy combinations, and SBRT-immunotherapy have demonstrated feasible delivery and meaningful pathological responses. KEYNOTE-689 established improved event-free survival with perioperative pembrolizumab. Postoperatively, cisplatin-radiotherapy remains standard for positive margins and extranodal extension, while NIVOPOST-OP supports nivolumab intensification in high-risk disease. Maintenance therapy remains uncertain, with negative MACE results but a possible benefit from tegafur-uracil in selected patients. CONCLUSION: Perioperative immunotherapy is reshaping resectable OSCC treatment. Postoperative intensification, maintenance therapy, and lower-dose strategies, including low-dose nivolumab with metronomic therapy, require prospective validation. These approaches may be especially important in resource-constrained settings, where treatment cost and access remain major barriers.
